text:
A: Hiya! Oh, it's you, I was hoping I'd get you. I spotted your sewing machine in your picture.
B: Ha, hello! Yes, that's my sewing machine, well spotted. I'm Rutendo.
A: Lisa. Sorry, I've jumped straight in there. Do you make your own clothes, then?
B: I do, yeah. Mostly from wax print, the African fabrics, and charity shop stuff. I'm halfway through a dress at the moment, actually. It's been halfway for about three weeks.
A: That's still more than me. I've got a cross-stitch I started in 2021. It's a robin. It's got about half a robin.
B: Half a robin is a start, you know?
A: That's what I tell Dean. He says it's a crime scene. So where are you, then?
B: Coventry. I've been here twenty years now, I moved over from Zimbabwe when I was nineteen. So Coventry's home, really.
A: Oh, lovely. I'm Ipswich, born and bred, never left. My whole family's within about twenty minutes. What do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
B: I'm an occupational therapist, for the council. Home visits mostly. Someone's had a stroke or a fall, or they're just getting older and struggling, and I go round and see what would help them stay at home safely. Rails, equipment, sometimes just moving the furniture about.
A: Oh, that's a lovely job. That's a proper job, that. I just do paperwork for shipping containers.
B: Paperwork keeps the world going, though. Somebody has to know where the containers are.
A: Ha, well, half the time I don't! Erm, can I ask you something, actually, since you do that? My mum's started getting a bit forgetful. Nothing major, she's just, she left the gas on the other week, and she's been putting things in the wrong cupboards. And I don't know if I'm worrying over nothing.
B: No, it's not nothing, it's good that you've noticed. The first thing really is getting her to the GP, just so it's on the record, even if it's just a check. And then there's lots of small things that help, honestly. Some cookers have an automatic cut-off, you can get labels for the cupboards, a big clock with the day on it. Sometimes it's the little things that keep people independent the longest.
A: A clock with the day on it. That's a good idea, she's always asking me what day it is.
B: Yeah. And if it gets more, your council will have an OT team like mine, you can ask for an assessment. It's free.
A: Oh, I didn't know that. Thank you, that's really kind. Sorry, I've made it all serious now.
B: No, no, I'm glad you asked. Most people don't, they wait till something's happened.
A: That's me, though, isn't it, last minute for everything. Erm, what do you do at the weekend? Bet you do something cultured.
B: Ha, sometimes. I go to the Herbert, the gallery, and the theatre. And I sing in the church choir on Sundays, alto. We're learning something really tricky for Easter at the moment.
A: Oh, I love that. I'm not in the choir but I do the church Christmas fair every year, I'm on the tombola. I'm not musical at all, I just sell raffle tickets to people who don't want them.
B: That's an important job too. Our fair would fall apart without the tombola people.
A: It's always the same five of us! Did you have the Welsh lad yet, Rhys? He's got a whippet that's scared of the bins.
B: Not yet, no. Scared of the bins?
A: Terrified. He has to carry it past. Every fortnight.
B: Oh, bless it. Our bins have changed days again, so I'd be just as confused as the
